title: India's 'Cockroach' Youth Protests Force Parliament Shutdown, Draw Celebrity Support
excerpt: Thousands of Gen Z protesters demanding the education minister's resignation over the NEET exam paper leak have clashed with police in Delhi, shut down metro stations, and drawn backing from Bollywood stars and opposition leaders.
body:
• Tens of thousands of protesters attempted to march on India's Parliament on July 20, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET-UG paper leak; police responded with tear gas and baton charges, injuring at least 180 people.
  • The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical youth movement born online in May 2026, has become the biggest public challenge to PM Modi in his third term.
  • Activist Sonam Wangchuk's 24-day hunger strike has galvanized the movement, with Bollywood actors including Diljit Dosanjh, Shabana Azmi, and Prakash Raj publicly supporting the students.
  • Parliament's monsoon session has been repeatedly disrupted, with 16 Delhi Metro stations closed and 20 CRPF companies airlifted to the capital.

A Gen Z Movement Takes on India's Government

The streets around New Delhi's 300-year-old Jantar Mantar observatory have become ground zero for what observers are calling India's largest anti-government demonstrations in years. The Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical movement that began as an Instagram page in May — has mobilized tens of thousands of mostly Gen Z protesters demanding accountability for a leaked national medical entrance exam.

On July 20, the opening day of Parliament's monsoon session, thousands of demonstrators attempted to march toward the Parliament building. Delhi Police, which had imposed prohibitory orders and denied permission for the march, responded with tear gas and baton charges. According to police, 118 officers were injured; the CJP said more than 150 protesters were hospitalized, with at least one requiring surgery for pellet wounds.

The Spark: A Paper Leak That Wrecked Millions of Futures

The crisis traces back to May, when a paper leak compromised the NEET-UG 2026 medical entrance examination, forcing some 2.2 million students to resit. At least 12 students died by suicide in the aftermath, according to media reports. The Central Bureau of Investigation has arrested 13 people in connection with the leak.

The movement's name references Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's remark comparing unemployed youth and social media activists to "cockroaches" — a statement the CJP's founder, digital strategist Abhijeet Dipke, repurposed as a rallying cry. The movement amassed millions of Instagram followers within days of being created.

"Students should not have been treated like this. I request the authorities to listen to the students' demands."

— Diljit Dosanjh, singer-actor

Wangchuk's Hunger Strike Becomes a Focal Point

Ladakhi environmentalist and education activist Sonam Wangchuk — the real-life inspiration for Aamir Khan's character in 3 Idiots — began an indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar on June 28. By his 19th day, he had lost 9.1 kilograms and could no longer stand unaided. On July 18, Delhi Police forcibly removed him from the protest site and admitted him to Safdarjung Hospital.

The Delhi High Court subsequently ordered Wangchuk transferred to Medanta Hospital in Gurugram. On Wednesday, he issued a letter saying he would end his fast only if the government gave "an unequivocal assurance" against retaliatory action on student protesters.

Bollywood Breaks Its Silence

The July 20 crackdown triggered a wave of celebrity support. Actors Shabana Azmi and Prakash Raj physically joined protesters at Jantar Mantar, while Diljit Dosanjh, Sonakshi Sinha, Bhumi Pednekar, Huma Qureshi, Riteish Deshmukh, Dia Mirza, and filmmaker Anurag Kashyap spoke out on social media.

"People will judge! When history will be written tomorrow, they may forgive who might have made the mistake but they will never forgive who was silent," actor Prakash Raj said in an interview, criticizing Bollywood's initial reluctance to take a stand.

Parliament and Government Respond

The protests have repeatedly disrupted Parliament's monsoon session, with opposition leaders raising the students' cause on the floor. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi was detained after protesting outside PM Modi's residence on July 21. Gandhi called Modi India's most "anti-youth Prime Minister."

Education Minister Pradhan broke his silence on Tuesday, saying the government was "100% committed to discussing NEET and addressing every genuine concern of our youth." Health Minister J.P. Nadda met CJP leaders and sought time to discuss their demands, which include Pradhan's resignation, Wangchuk's release, and compensation of ₹1 crore ($104,000) for each student who died by suicide.

The government deployed 20 CRPF companies airlifted from Kolkata to Delhi, shut down 16 metro stations across central Delhi, and cut internet service in the vicinity of Parliament.

A Movement With Staying Power

For India's diaspora, the protests echo a familiar pattern of youth frustration. The NEET leak is the latest in a string of examination scandals — at least 345 paper leaks over 28 years, according to protest organizers. High youth unemployment and a competitive exam system that determines life trajectories have created a pressure cooker that the CJP has channeled into sustained street action.

Demonstrations have now spread to Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Goa, and other cities. Solidarity rallies have been held outside Indian diplomatic missions in London, Dublin, New York, and San Jose. As thousands remain camped at Jantar Mantar in the rain, the movement's leaders say they will not leave until their demands are met.
image_caption: Protesters gather at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi during the Cockroach Janta Party's ongoing demonstrations against the NEET paper leak. The site, a historic observatory turned protest ground, has been the movement's headquarters since June 2026.
nri_angle: The NEET scandal and youth unemployment crisis resonate deeply with diaspora families whose children face similar examination pressures, while solidarity rallies in London, New York, and San Jose show the movement's global reach
author: Diaspora Desk
